entityDossier.whatItIs: STAR GATE was the final code name for a U.S. government psychic-intelligence effort that ran from roughly 1970 to 1995 under a rotating series of names and host agencies: SCANATE (CIA-funded, from 1970), GONDOLA WISH (Army ACSI, 1977), GRILL FLAME (Army INSCOM Detachment G at Fort Meade, 1978), INSCOM CENTER LANE (1983), SUN STREAK (DIA Scientific and Technical Intelligence Directorate, office code DT-S, 1985), and STAR GATE (DIA with SAIC as prime contractor, 1991). It combined an operational collection unit that tasked trained remote viewers against real intelligence targets with a separately maintained contract research program run out of Stanford Research Institute. It was terminated in 1995 after a Congressionally Directed Action moved it to CIA and CIA declined to keep it.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: STAR GATE is the board's cleanest declassified proof-of-concept for the exact institutional pattern the legacy program is alleged to follow: a real, funded, operational, compartmented effort into a phenomenon the government publicly treated as nonsense, sustained across two decades and at least four host organizations by serial renaming, moved between Army, DIA and CIA in a way that defeats continuity of oversight, and run through a cleared contractor (SRI, then SAIC) rather than in-house. The 1995 CIA program-status memorandum shows the disposal mechanics with unusual clarity: CIA and DIA had already made 'plans to declassify all but the most sensitive aspects of the program' before any evaluation was complete, and the memo's author recommended asking Congress to agree the program should NOT transfer to CIA before the contracted review had even begun. That is a decision to terminate reached in advance of the evidence, followed by a curated declassification, which means the archive the public got is the residue of a deliberate sorting operation rather than a data dump. The program also demonstrates that a phenomenon-adjacent effort could be carried in the black for twenty-five years while officials denied its existence, and that its closure could be framed publicly as a scientific verdict rather than a bureaucratic one. Finally, STAR GATE is a personnel bridge: the scientists, contractors and case officers it credentialed are the same names that reappear in the NIDS, AAWSAP and To The Stars-era record, giving the board a documented lineage from Cold War compartmented research to the 2017-2026 disclosure fight.
entityDossier.narrative:
The origin story is threat-mirroring. Between 1969 and 1971, U.S. intelligence concluded the Soviet Union was investing seriously in what it called psychotronics, with estimates running to 60 million rubles per year by 1970 and over 300 million by 1975. Whether or not the Soviets had anything, the money itself was treated as evidence, and CIA opened a research line in 1970 under the name SCANATE. In 1972 the research moved to Stanford Research Institute in Menlo Park, where Russell Targ and Harold Puthoff ran it, initially around a small set of gifted individuals including the artist Ingo Swann. The client requirement, per the FAS program file, was a minimum accuracy of 65 percent.

The operational side grew separately out of the Army. GONDOLA WISH, a 1977 Army Assistant Chief of Staff for Intelligence effort under the Systems Exploitation Detachment, was chartered to evaluate potential adversary applications of remote viewing. It became a collection project in mid-1978 as GRILL FLAME, INSCOM 'Detachment G,' housed in buildings 2560 and 2561 at Fort Meade, Maryland. The SRI research was folded into GRILL FLAME in early 1979, and hundreds of experiments were run at SRI through 1986. Renamed the INSCOM CENTER LANE Project in 1983, the unit adopted a written methodology developed by Swann and Puthoff meant to make the capability trainable rather than innate. Its existence surfaced publicly when columnist Jack Anderson reported on it in April 1984. That same year the National Academy of Sciences' National Research Council evaluated remote viewing for the Army Research Institute and returned an unfavorable verdict. When Army funding ended in late 1985, the unit did not die; it was redesignated SUN STREAK and moved to DIA's Scientific and Technical Intelligence Directorate under office code DT-S. In 1991 the contract moved to Science Applications International Corporation and the program became STAR GATE, downgraded from a Special Access Program to a LIMDIS, limited dissemination, program. Edwin May presided over roughly 70 percent of the total contractor budget and 85 percent of data collection. Over two decades the effort consumed on the order of $20 million, with about $11 million spent from the mid-1980s to the early 1990s, and involved more than forty personnel including about twenty-three remote viewers.

The end is where the concealment mechanics are legible. The FY1995 Defense Appropriations bill directed transfer to CIA and directed CIA to conduct a retrospective review. What happened next is documented in a SECRET memorandum, 'Star Gate - Program Status and Proposed New Direction,' now in the CIA reading room as CIA-RDP96-00791R000100160001-0. The Executive Director approved CIA's approach in late January 1995; it was transmitted to Congress and briefed to Richard D'Amato of the Senate Appropriations Committee staff on 27 March 1995. CIA transferred funds to the Army Research Institute to make it executive agent for a National Research Council blue-ribbon review. In parallel, and this is the sentence that matters for the board, CIA was 'working closely with DIA and their support contractor to identify all relevant documents pertaining to Star Gate' and had 'made plans to declassify all but the most sensitive aspects of the program.' The sorting of what the public would eventually see was underway before the verdict was in.

NRC declined the review by letter dated 5 May 1995, citing its own 1988 report and quoting its conclusion that the case for remote viewing was 'not just very weak, but virtually nonexistent.' NRC referred CIA to Dr. David Goslin, president of the American Institutes for Research. The memo's author then recommended skipping the review entirely: 'in view of the strong position taken by the NRC... I want to propose at this point that we strongly consider the option of going back to Congress with the recommendation not to accept the Star Gate program from DIA,' adding that even if AIR proceeded 'there exists a very strong possibility that AIR will merely reach the same conclusion firmly held by the NRC.' He also recorded that 'neither the DO nor the DI were at all interested in having this program reside in their directorates,' and deferred any decision about the operational personnel still at DIA. The recommendation was explicit: 'ask Congress to agree that the program should NOT be transferred to CIA.'

AIR did the review anyway. Its final report is dated 29 September 1995 and was released publicly on 28 November 1995. It contained two irreconcilable assessments, statistician Jessica Utts finding a statistically significant laboratory effect and psychologist Ray Hyman finding none, and a single recommendation to terminate. CIA's public line was that there was no case in which ESP had provided data used to guide intelligence operations. The program had been sustained politically for years by Senator Claiborne Pell of Rhode Island and Representative Charles Rose of North Carolina; with the program dead, the constituency dissolved.

What the board should take from STAR GATE is not whether remote viewing worked. It is the demonstrated administrative repertoire: serial renaming across host commands, movement between Army, DIA and CIA, SAP-to-LIMDIS reclassification, contractor intermediation, a pre-cooked termination decision, a curated declassification, and a public verdict framed in the language of science rather than of budget politics. Every one of those moves is available to any program that wants to disappear while remaining funded, and every one is documented here in the government's own paper.

entityDossier.whatItIs: A nine-page unclassified intelligence product titled 'Preliminary Assessment: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena,' issued by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence on 25 June 2021 in response to a provision in Senate Report 116-233 accompanying the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021. It was drafted by the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force and the ODNI National Intelligence Manager for Aviation, with input from sixteen named agencies and components, and prepared for the Congressional Intelligence and Armed Services Committees. It reviewed 144 U.S. Government UAP reports from November 2004 to March 2021 and resolved exactly one.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: This is the document in which the U.S. Intelligence Community, in writing and on the record, declined to attribute a single one of 143 unresolved incidents to American classified programs, and admitted it could not confirm that its own developmental programs accounted for any of them. That admission cuts both ways and the board should hold both edges. If the objects are not U.S. black programs, the IC has just conceded 143 unexplained penetrations of restricted airspace, many near nuclear-capable and test infrastructure. If they are U.S. black programs, then the DNI's own coordinating body was denied read-in access to them, which is the definition of the concealment the board asserts. The assessment further records that UAP cluster around U.S. training and testing grounds and near facilities carrying the most advanced sensor systems, that in eighteen incidents observers reported unusual flight characteristics, that military aircraft systems processed radio-frequency energy associated with sightings, and that the task force holds data appearing to show acceleration or signature management. It is also a concealment artifact in its own right: it names the accountable official only by title, ships the substance to a classified annex, and defines the problem as a data-collection deficiency rather than an access deficiency, converting a question about who is hiding what into a request for better forms and more money.
entityDossier.narrative:
The assessment exists because of a paragraph in a Senate committee report, not because of an executive decision to inform the public. Senate Report 116-233, submitted by Senator Marco Rubio from the Select Committee on Intelligence on 17 June 2020 to accompany S. 3905, directed the DNI, in consultation with the Secretary of Defense, to submit an intelligence assessment of the threat posed by UAP and of the progress the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force had made. Appendix B of the resulting product reprints the eight specific things the Senate asked for. Two of them are worth memorizing. Item 4 demanded 'a detailed description of an interagency process for ensuring timely data collection and centralized analysis of all UAP reporting for the Federal Government, regardless of which service or agency acquired the information.' Item 5 demanded 'Identification of an official accountable for the process described in paragraph 4.' The Senate was asking, in oversight language, who owns the file. ODNI's answer, in the Scope section, is a title with no name attached: 'The Director, UAPTF, is the accountable official for ensuring the timely collection and consolidation of data on UAP.'

The drafting coalition is itself a finding. The report was written by the UAPTF and the ODNI National Intelligence Manager for Aviation, with input from USD(I&S), DIA, FBI, NRO, NGA, NSA, Air Force, Army, Navy, Navy/ONI, DARPA, FAA, NOAA, ODNI/NIM-Emerging and Disruptive Technology, ODNI's National Counterintelligence and Security Center, and the National Intelligence Council. The Department of Energy is not on the list. Neither is CIA. Neither is any Special Access Program Central Office. For a document whose central unresolved question is whether the objects are American, the absence of the organizations that would custody the most sensitive American aerospace and nuclear-adjacent programs is the shape of the hole.

The numbers are small and precise. One hundred forty-four reports originated from USG sources. Eighty of those involved observation with multiple sensors: radar, infrared, electro-optical, weapon seekers, visual. One was identified with high confidence, 'a large, deflating balloon.' The rest, 143, 'remain unexplained.' In eighteen incidents, described across twenty-one reports, observers reported unusual movement or flight characteristics: objects that appeared to remain stationary in winds aloft, move against the wind, maneuver abruptly, or travel at considerable speed 'without discernable means of propulsion.' In a small number of cases 'military aircraft systems processed radio frequency (RF) energy associated with UAP sightings.' The UAPTF 'holds a small amount of data that appear to show UAP demonstrating acceleration or a degree of signature management,' with further analysis promised. Eleven documented near misses were on file.

The five-bin taxonomy, airborne clutter, natural atmospheric phenomena, USG or industry developmental programs, foreign adversary systems, and a catchall 'other,' is where the board plants its flag. Under the third bin the report says: 'Some UAP observations could be attributable to developments and classified programs by U.S. entities. We were unable to confirm, however, that these systems accounted for any of the UAP reports we collected.' That is not a denial that such programs exist. It is a statement that the drafters could not obtain confirmation. An intelligence assessment written by the DNI's aviation manager and coordinated across sixteen organizations was unable to check its own government's classified aerospace inventory against its own government's unexplained-object file. Either no such inventory exists, or access to it was refused, or the query was never seriously pressed. Each possibility is load-bearing.

The geographic finding is handled the same way. UAP sightings 'tended to cluster around U.S. training and testing grounds,' and 'some UAP have been detected near military facilities or by aircraft carrying the USG's most advanced sensor systems.' The report immediately neutralizes this as probable collection bias: more sensors, greater expectation, standing guidance to report anomalies. That may be true. It is also exactly the explanation one would offer to avoid the alternative reading, which is that the objects are interested in specific American infrastructure, the same pattern documented at Loring, Wurtsmith, Malmstrom, Minot and Falconbridge in October and November 1975.

The remedies proposed are all inputs, never access. Standardize reporting. Consolidate data. Employ artificial intelligence and machine learning to cluster features. Search historical radar archives with advanced algorithms. Update the interagency collection strategy. Increase R&D investment guided by a UAP Collection Strategy, a UAP R&D Technical Roadmap, and a UAP Program Plan. Not one recommendation asks any agency to disclose what it already holds. The report also records, candidly, that no standardized reporting mechanism existed anywhere in the U.S. military until the Navy created one in March 2019 and the Air Force adopted it in November 2020, meaning that for the entire post-Blue Book era the United States operated with no formal channel by which a military aviator could report an object over a nuclear or test facility. That is not an accident of bureaucracy; it is a design decision with a fifty-year half-life. The report is equally candid about the human cost: aviators and analysts 'describe disparagement associated with observing UAP, reporting it, or attempting to discuss it with colleagues.'

The institutional sequel followed within six months. Section 1683 of the FY2022 National Defense Authorization Act, Public Law 117-81, signed 27 December 2021, directed establishment of a successor office. The Airborne Object Identification and Management Synchronization Group was stood up and then superseded; the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office was formally established by a Deputy Secretary of Defense memorandum published 20 July 2022, designating AARO the authoritative DoD focal point for UAP and placing it under USD(I&S), one of the very components that had contributed to this assessment. The task force that could not confirm whether American programs accounted for any of its own 144 cases was thereby replaced by an office that would go on to assert that no such programs ever existed. The 2021 assessment is the last moment the U.S. government's written position was uncertainty rather than denial, which is precisely why it is the most useful single document in the modern record.

entityDossier.whatItIs: The Department of Defense's annual department-wide financial statement audit, first performed for fiscal year 2018 and repeated every year since, coordinated by the DoD Office of Inspector General across dozens of component audits. It has never produced a clean opinion. DoD is the only major federal agency that has never received an unmodified audit opinion on its financial statements, and its balance sheet is assembled through summary-level accounting adjustments, journal vouchers, that auditors have repeatedly found to be unsupported by documentation traceable to actual transactions.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: This is the financial-concealment thread and it requires no exotic assumption. If a department cannot demonstrate where more than four trillion dollars in reported assets sits, cannot reconcile its subsidiary systems to its general ledger, and closes the gap each quarter with trillions of dollars in undocumented journal vouchers, then the accounting system itself functions as a laundering mechanism whether or not anyone designed it that way. Money moved into an unacknowledged program does not need a fake line item; it needs only to enter an environment where the difference between the books and reality is routinely papered over at a scale that dwarfs the transaction. The DoD Inspector General documented $6.5 trillion in unsupported year-end adjustments and $2.8 trillion in unsupported third-quarter adjustments to the Army General Fund in a single fiscal year against an Army budget of roughly $120 billion. GAO has found that identified material weaknesses directly affect over half of DoD's reported assets. The audit failure is therefore not merely a governance embarrassment; it is the enabling condition for any funding stream the board alleges. It also functions as an oversight artifact with a deadline: Congress has now set a statutory requirement for a clean opinion by 31 December 2028, which for the first time gives concealment a dated, enforceable test to fail.
entityDossier.narrative:
Start with the number that made the pattern famous. DoD Inspector General Report No. DODIG-2016-113, 'Army General Fund Adjustments Not Adequately Documented or Supported,' issued 26 July 2016, found that Army and Defense Finance and Accounting Service Indianapolis personnel did not adequately support $2.8 trillion in third-quarter adjustments and $6.5 trillion in year-end adjustments made to Army General Fund data during the fiscal year 2015 financial statement compilation. The Army's entire enacted budget that year was on the order of $120 billion. The unsupported year-end adjustments were therefore roughly fifty-four times the money Congress actually authorized the Army to spend.

The mechanism deserves precision, because the scale invites dismissal. A journal voucher is a summary-level accounting entry made when balances between two systems will not reconcile. It is legitimate when it is documented and tied to identifiable transactions. It is what auditors call a plug when it is not. DoD's feeder systems for procurement, logistics, personnel and property were never built to talk to its accounting systems, so at each reporting cycle the difference is closed by hand. The Inspector General's finding was not that the Army stole $6.5 trillion. It was that the Army could not demonstrate what the adjustments represented. From an audit standpoint those are functionally identical: unsupported entries at that magnitude mean the books cannot be used to detect anything, including diversion.

This was not new in 2016. Reuters correspondent Scot J. Paltrow's 2013 investigative series 'Unaccountable: The High Cost of the Pentagon's Bad Bookkeeping,' culminating in a special report published 18 November 2013, documented that fabricating entries to force agreement was standard operating procedure at DFAS offices handling the Army, Navy, Air Force and other defense agencies, and cited a December 2011 Pentagon Inspector General report finding that a single DFAS office in Columbus, Ohio had made at least $1.59 trillion in errors, including $538 billion in plugs, in fiscal year 2009 Air Force financial reports.

The modern audit era begins with fiscal year 2018, the first full-scope department-wide audit. It has failed every year since. For fiscal year 2024, GAO reported that DoD received a disclaimer of opinion for the seventh consecutive year, meaning DoD could not provide auditors sufficient, appropriate evidence to support the information in its financial statements, owing to ineffective systems and processes. DoD reported over $4.1 trillion in assets on its balance sheet as of 30 September 2024. That balance sheet consolidated information from sixty-seven separate DoD components. Eleven components received clean opinions, contributing $1.8 trillion of reported assets, 42.8 percent, and $3.1 trillion of reported liabilities, 72.2 percent. But GAO added the detail that guts the headline: nearly all of the assets attributable to clean-opinion components related to the Military Retirement Fund, a pension trust, while nearly all assets attributable to disclaimer components related to the Army, Navy and Air Force. The parts of DoD that can be audited are the parts that do not buy anything.

The DoD Office of Inspector General identified twenty-eight department-wide material weaknesses for fiscal year 2024. GAO's own analysis found that several of those DoD-wide material weaknesses directly affected $2.1 trillion of DoD's reported assets, 50.3 percent, and $146.9 billion of reported liabilities, 3.4 percent, and cautioned that pervasive material weaknesses may affect all balance sheet data. Congressional Research Service analysis of the FY2024 results adds that entities receiving disclaimers accounted for 44 percent of DoD's total assets and at least 68 percent of its total budgetary resources, and that DoD extended the target date for correcting its department-wide financial management systems modernization material weakness from FY2028 to FY2031, a slippage past the statutory audit deadline itself.

That deadline is the newest and most useful fact for the board. The National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024 requires DoD to receive an unmodified audit opinion by 31 December 2028; CRS identifies the provision as Section 1005. GAO states the requirement flatly in GAO-25-108052. The department has therefore been given a legal obligation to become legible on a specific date, while simultaneously moving its own systems-modernization fix three years past that date.

The fiscal year 2025 cycle continued the pattern. The DoD Office of Inspector General issued Report No. DODIG-2026-032, 'Independent Auditor's Reports on the DoD FY 2025 Financial Statements,' comprising three separate audit reports addressing the financial statements, internal control over financial reporting, and compliance with laws and regulations. What this means for the legacy-program argument is narrow and strong. It does not prove that money was diverted. It proves that DoD's accounting environment cannot rule out diversion at any scale below the noise floor, and that the noise floor is measured in trillions. Every other funding hypothesis on the board, whether contractor-held Independent Research and Development recovery, unacknowledged Special Access Programs, waived SAPs briefed only to a handful of members, or overhead absorption on classified contracts, sits downstream of one structural fact: the Department of Defense's books do not close, have never closed, and the entries that make them appear to close are, by the Inspector General's own finding, undocumented. Executed under 15 U.S.C. section 3710a with a term of sixty months from the effective date, it committed TTSA to provide the Army with samples of metamaterial 'collected, obtained, or developed as part of its Field Operations' and the Army to provide laboratories, expertise and analysis, with no exchange of funds in either direction. TTSA's principal investigator of record was Luis Elizondo.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: This is the only publicly released, signed U.S. Government instrument in which a federal laboratory agrees to characterize material that the counterparty represented, in filings to the Securities and Exchange Commission, as coming from unidentified aerial phenomena. That makes it the board's hardest documentary bridge between the alleged recovery-and-exploitation enterprise and the ordinary federal technology-transfer system. The Joint Work Plan names the Government's actual interests, and the list is not generic materials science: 'inertial mass reduction, mechanical/structural metamaterials, electromagnetic metamaterial wave guides, quantum physics, quantum communications, and beamed energy propulsion.' Inertial mass reduction is not a ground-vehicle survivability requirement. The Collaborator principal investigator is Luis Elizondo, the former Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence official associated with AATIP who left DoD in 2017 alleging excessive secrecy, meaning the same individual who publicly accused the Pentagon of concealment is, two years later, the named point of contact delivering anomalous material back into an Army laboratory under an agreement whose supporting records the Department of Defense then withheld under national-defense FOIA exemptions. Finally, the CRADA form itself is the point: it moves technology and creates invention rights without appropriated funds, without a contract, without competition and without a reportable obligation, and it carries a statutory information shield. It is a legal channel for moving exploitable material into and out of the Government that leaves almost no financial footprint.
entityDossier.narrative:
On 17 October 2019 To The Stars Academy of Arts & Science issued a press release announcing a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement with the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command to develop enhanced capabilities for Army ground vehicles. The release was thin. The Army was not. Doug Halleaux, public affairs officer for CCDC's Ground Vehicle Systems Center, gave John Greenewald of The Black Vault the executed agreement, twenty-six pages, redacted only for phone numbers.

The document is CRADA No. 19-15, 'Novel & Emerging Technology Exploitation (NETE),' between TTSA and CCDC Ground Vehicle Systems Center, 6501 E. 11 Mile Road, Warren, Michigan. The named administrators matter. On the Government side the principal investigators are Ben Soave and Dr. Joseph Cannon, both of Ground Vehicle Survivability and Protection, mail stop 263b. The ORTA representative is Andrea Simon; Government legal counsel is Christina Dellmore, Chief of the Intellectual Property Law Division at US Army TACOM LCMC. On the Collaborator side, the principal investigator and preferred contact is Luis Elizondo, 'Director of Global Security and Special Programs,' Encinitas, California. Collaborator legal counsel is Heidy Vaquerano, Esq., of Wolf, Rifkin, Shapiro, Schulman & Rabkin, LLP, Los Angeles.

The Joint Work Plan is where the agreement stops sounding like armor research. The Government's stated interests are 'a variety of the Collaborator's technologies, such as, but not limited to inertial mass reduction, mechanical/structural metamaterials, electromagnetic metamaterial wave guides, quantum physics, quantum communications, and beamed energy propulsion.' The Collaborator's deliverables include, verbatim, 'Metamaterial: Samples of mechanical and EM sensitive metamaterial collected, obtained, or developed as part of its Field Operations,' plus written material analysis and quantum-communication research. 'Field Operations' is the operative euphemism; the CRADA does not define provenance, and the Army made a point of saying provenance was irrelevant to it.

The legal architecture is standard Federal Technology Transfer Act plumbing put to non-standard use. Information exchanged is protected under 15 U.S.C. section 3710a(c)(7), and every page carries a marking legend invoking it. Licenses to CRADA inventions run under 15 U.S.C. section 3710a(b)(2), with the Collaborator holding an option for an exclusive license that must be requested within six months of notification of an invention. The agreement automatically expires sixty months from the effective date under Article 4.2, and enters force on the date signed by the last authorized representative under Article 4.3.

TTSA's own SEC filings supply the numbers the CRADA does not. In its Regulation A offering circular the company states that on 10 October 2019 it entered into the CRADA with CCDC, that 'the purpose of the CRADA is to advance developments in material science (including testing of the metamaterials), space-time metric engineering, quantum physics, beamed energy propulsion and active camouflage,' that the parties bear their own costs, that the total value of anticipated U.S. Government resources including personnel, services, intellectual property, facilities, equipment and reporting is 'estimated at $750,000,' that the total value of the company's participation is 'estimated at $1,000,000,' and that the agreement is terminable by mutual consent or unilaterally on thirty days' notice.

The same filing describes where the material came from. The ADAM Research Project, Acquisition and Data Analysis of Materials, launched in July 2018, and 'within one year this division acquired a collection of material samples reported to come from advanced vehicles of unknown origin from all over the world.' In July 2019 the company 'purchased multiple pieces of metamaterials and an archive of initial analysis and research.' Elsewhere TTSA states flatly to the SEC: 'The exotic materials that were purchased come from unidentified aerial phenomenon and are anomalous in that they have a structure and composition that we believe are unknown to any existing commercial or military application.' By November 2019, per the filing, ETI had performed analysis pursuant to the SOW-MSSA showing 'a unique physical structure unknown to any past or current commercial or military application.' The filing also records that planned ADAM laboratory testing 'was paused.'

The Army's public framing was deliberately deflationary. Halleaux told The Black Vault that 'the Army is providing the expertise and facilities to analyze the materials, and TTSA is providing the materials themselves; both parties receive the results of the analysis,' and that 'just as there is no financial compensation to TTSA for the use of the materials, there is no financial compensation to the Army for the use of the facilities.' On provenance he was explicit: 'the Army's interest is in the potential for novel materials and exploring the edges of materials science, any speculation as to their origin is (pardon the pun) immaterial.' He also stressed that a CRADA is not an endorsement, offering the Army's fuel-cell CRADA with General Motors as the comparison.

Then the record closed. Individuals who had custody of pieces of the metamaterial before TTSA acquired them were placed under non-disclosure agreements; The Black Vault reached one such person, who declined comment citing an NDA. Some of the material was described in SEC filings as being 'on loan.' The Department of Defense invoked FOIA exemptions covering national defense and foreign policy to withhold CRADA-related documents. It took until October 2024, five years after execution and at the natural end of the sixty-month term, before the Army agreed to a rolling release under FOIA case FA-24-0006, with the first package released on 23 October 2024.

The analytic point for the board is the instrument, not the rock. A CRADA requires no appropriation, no competition, no contract file and no reportable obligation, and carries a statutory information shield. It creates a lawful, low-visibility conduit for moving materials of undeclared origin into a federal laboratory and moving analysis and invention rights back out, with the collaborator holding a first option on exclusive rights to anything invented. Whatever the metamaterial turns out to be, CRADA 19-15 is the working proof that the channel exists, is routine, and is FOIA-resistant by design.

entityDossier.whatItIs: A sustained series of unidentified aerial incursions over Strategic Air Command nuclear weapons storage areas, bomber alert facilities and ICBM fields between 27 October and roughly 19 November 1975, at Loring AFB in Maine, Wurtsmith AFB in Michigan, Malmstrom AFB in Montana, Minot AFB in North Dakota, and Canadian Forces Station Falconbridge in Ontario. The events generated OPREP messages to the National Military Command Center, a SAC-wide security directive, NORAD Senior Director's Log entries, repeated failed interceptor scrambles, and a five-part CINCNORAD message dated 11 November 1975. Most of the documentary record entered the public domain through FOIA requests filed by civilian researchers between 1976 and 1978.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: This is the best-documented case in the entire record of sustained, deliberate interest by unidentified objects in American nuclear weapons infrastructure, and the government's own contemporaneous words are the evidence. An Air Force operational report stated that the intruder 'has demonstrated a clear intent in the weapons storage area.' SAC issued a directive to ten northern-tier bases under the subject line 'Defense Against Helicopter Assault,' placing them at Security Option 3 during hours of darkness. The commander of NORAD told his own command that Falconbridge personnel observed through binoculars a '100 ft. diameter sphere' that 'appeared to have craters around the outside' at altitudes between 26,000 and 72,000 feet, and in the same message wrote that he had 'expressed my concern to SAFOI that we come up soonest with a proposed answer to queries from the press to prevent overreaction by the public.' That is a dated, attributable instruction to build a press posture before the identification problem was solved, the concealment effort visible in real time in the commander's own sentence. Three years later, when a subcommittee chairman finally asked for the records, the Air Force replied in writing that it could find no official information and that some of the incidents 'may not have happened at all,' then reversed and produced material while asserting that UFO reports are 'of transitory interest to the Air Force and permanent files are not maintained.' The 1975 wave therefore supplies four elements at once: intrusion on nuclear custody, total failure of interception, an explicit press-management decision, and a documented policy of non-retention that forecloses future audit.
entityDossier.narrative:
Loring Air Force Base in northern Maine was Strategic Air Command's easternmost continental installation, home to a B-52 squadron on nuclear alert and two KC-135 tanker squadrons, with a separately fenced nuclear weapons storage area. On the evening of 27 October 1975 security personnel observed what was officially recorded as 'an unidentified helicopter' near the northern perimeter at roughly 150 feet, showing a red navigation light and a white strobe, apparently interested in the weapons storage area. Army National Guard helicopters were dispatched and could not identify it. Control tower radar picked up a second unknown circling ten to thirteen miles northeast. The first turned north into Canada near Grand Falls, New Brunswick; the second vanished from the scope.

The following night it returned without lights. The operational report issued afterward contained the sentence that gave Fawcett and Greenwood's book its title: 'It is our opinion that the unknown helicopter has demonstrated a clear intent in the weapons storage area, is smart and a most capable aviator.' On 28 October, Sgt. Clifton W. Blakeslee, Staff Sgt. William J. Long and Sgt. Danny Lewis of the 42nd Security Police Squadron tracked an object for thirty-five minutes visually and on tower radar; the commander of the 42nd Bomb Wing observed it himself. Separately, B-52 crew chief Sgt. Steven Eichner and Sgt. R. Jones came within about 300 feet of a reddish-orange object roughly four car lengths long, hovering five feet off the ground without sound, with no visible doors, windows, propellers or engines. Priority messages went to the National Military Command Center, the Chief of Staff of the Air Force, Fort Ritchie, SAC Headquarters and the 9th Air Force, advising that an unknown object had penetrated the base and had been in the nuclear storage area.

Security Police Shift Commander Arthur Beers later described a call from the National Emergency Command Post, with a colonel ordering him to shoot the helicopter down if it buzzed the area again; minutes later a general officer said the President had been briefed and the orders were changed to shoot only if it attempted to land. Chief Warrant Officer Bernard Poulin of the Maine Army National Guard flew UH-1 search missions vectored to where the object was being seen and heard, and never acquired it. Poulin recalled the base commander saying, 'We've got to keep the lid on the fact that someone has been able to penetrate in and around the bomb dump, and we don't know what's going on.'

SAC escalated laterally. A SAC Security Police message subject-lined 'Defense Against Helicopter Assault' went to ten northern-tier bases from Pease to Barksdale, directing them to 'assume Security Option 3 during hours of darkness until further notice.'

On 30 October it was Wurtsmith's turn. Security police at the back gate reported at 10:14, 10:20 and 10:25 p.m. an unidentified craft with no lights hovering low over the weapons storage area. RAPCON tracked it roughly thirty-five miles southeast over Lake Huron and the wing commander ordered a returning KC-135 to identify. Instructor navigator Capt. Myron Taylor's 'Memo for the Record' of 18 January 1979, written for 379th Bomb Wing historian SSgt Paul J. Cahill, records the pursuit: 'each time we attempted to close on the object it would speed away from us... I would estimate that the UFO sped away from us doing approximately 1,000 knots.' Taylor also recorded that about a week later the aircraft commander, Capt. Higginbotham, was questioned by OSI and 'cautioned not to discuss the incident.' On 31 October the Air Force Intelligence Service Alert Officer's Log recorded: 'Per Ltc. Redican's direction. Contacted DIA OPS center and informed them of unidentified flight activity over two SAC bases near Canadian border.'

Malmstrom's turn came 7 and 8 November, in the missile fields. On 10 November Minot Air Force Station logged 'a bright star-like object in the west, moving east, about the size of a car,' which 'passed over the radar station, 1000-2000 feet high, no noise heard.' On the morning of 11 November, CFS Falconbridge held radar paints thirty nautical miles south of the site between 26,000 and 72,000 feet; two F-106s from Selfridge ANGB were scrambled and made no contact.

That same day the Commander-in-Chief of NORAD sent a five-part message to NORAD units across North America. Part I named the five installations. Part II recorded that Malmstrom radars carried an object between 9,500 and 15,600 feet at seven knots, that F-106s could not make contact, that site personnel reported the object as low as 200 feet, and that 'as the interceptors approached the lights went out. After the interceptors had passed the lights came on again.' Part IV recorded the Falconbridge '100 ft. diameter sphere' with 'craters around the outside.' Part V is the concealment sentence: 'I have also expressed my concern to SAFOI that we come up soonest with a proposed answer to queries from the press to prevent overreaction by the public to reports by the media that may be blown out of proportion. To date efforts by Air Guard helicopters, SAC helicopters and Norad F-106s have failed to produce positive ID.'

Congress learned about it three years late and from a magazine. Parade published 'UFO's vs. USAF' by Michael Satchell on 10 December 1978. Representative Samuel S. Stratton (D-NY), chairman of the Armed Services Investigations Subcommittee, wrote to Maj. Gen. Charles C. Blanton on 20 December 1978 demanding all Air Force reports. The Air Force Directorate of Operations and Readiness responded internally on 8 January 1979: 'We have been unable to find any official information regarding the incidents described in the Parade magazine article... some of these incidents may not have happened at all.' On 9 February 1979 Joseph J. F. Clark, Associate Director of Legislative Liaison, produced a partial compilation and explained its thinness: 'unidentified flying object reports are of transitory interest to the Air Force and permanent files are not maintained.' Stratton did not pursue the matter further. The oversight window opened and closed in seven weeks.

entityDossier.whatItIs: A review conducted by the Office of the Chief Science Advisor of Canada into how public reports of unidentified aerial phenomena are handled by the Canadian federal government, published in June 2025 as a 59-page report titled 'Management of Public Reporting of Unidentified Aerial Phenomena in Canada,' carrying a message signed by Chief Science Advisor Mona Nemer. It surveyed federal departments, national and local police, civil aviation, the Coast Guard, citizen-science organizations and international comparators, and issued fourteen recommendations across reporting and data oversight, communications, research, and international collaboration.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: The Sky Canada Project is the board's cleanest documentation of concealment-by-non-recording, and it was written by a government about itself. Its central finding is that no Canadian federal body holds the UAP file: the RCMP has no policy, no classification and therefore no statistics; Transport Canada logs UAP into an aviation-safety database as an incidental category and does not investigate absent a safety concern; the RCAF does not investigate outside a threat or distress context; the National Research Council stopped collecting in 1995 and shipped fifteen thousand pages to the archives. Where no organization is responsible for a category of event, the absence of evidence is manufactured rather than observed, and every subsequent official statement that there is nothing to report becomes structurally true and evidentially worthless. The report also documents a measurable narrowing: direct submission of UAP reports from Canadian federal departments to independent researcher Chris Rutkowski, running since 2000, 'decreased significantly' by 2020, precisely as the American record was reopening. And it establishes the historical pattern, because Canada ran two named federal UAP programs, Project Magnet and Project Second Storey, and closed both on a committee finding that UFOs 'neither posed a security threat, nor were of scientific interest,' the Canadian twin of the Robertson Panel logic. Finally, it is an ally-government artifact that treats AARO as a model and recommends formal partnership with it, showing how the American framing is exported into allied policy.
entityDossier.narrative:
Canada's federal engagement with the phenomenon is older than most assume and was twice institutionalized and twice shut down. In 1950 the Department of Transport granted engineer Wilbert Smith permission to research whether some UFOs might use the power of the Earth's magnetic field as a source of propulsion. That was Project Magnet. Smith expanded its scope to include validating UFO observations, launched a balloon over Ottawa to monitor public and media reaction, and established a UFO observatory outside the capital. The department terminated Project Magnet in 1954 and Smith continued privately. In 1952 the Defence Research Board established Project Second Storey, chaired by National Research Council astronomer Dr. Peter Millman with members from Canadian military intelligence and other agencies. Second Storey did not investigate sightings. It produced a reporting form that was never broadly adopted, met six times between 1952 and 1954, concluded that 'UFOs neither posed a security threat, nor were of scientific interest,' and recommended ending all investigations by the Canadian military. That recommendation held for seventy years.

From 1954 to 1967 reports drifted to the RCMP, Transport Canada, National Defence and local police, occasionally logged, never systematized. In 1967, on the recommendation of the Minister of National Defence, the file went to the National Research Council, a transfer that included declassification of both Second Storey and Magnet. Millman personally answered public queries, usually with stars, planets, meteors and optical phenomena. In 1995 the NRC stopped collecting altogether and everything went to Library and Archives Canada, where the collection sits today at an estimated fifteen thousand pages, of which some nine thousand five hundred have been digitized. Over the last decade the NRC has processed only about forty UAP-related inquiries.

That is the vacuum the Sky Canada Project stepped into, and its consultations produced admissions more useful than any sighting. The RCMP, which serves roughly seventy-three percent of Canada's landmass and holds a federal investigative mandate nationwide, told the OCSA it has no formal policy for collection or dissemination of UAP reports and no classification system specific to UAPs, and that such reports are typically categorized as non-offence incidents under 'Aeronautics Act - Other Activities,' a bucket that also holds drone sightings. There is no guidance for call takers; a UAP call can be logged as a 'suspicious vehicle' and lost. The report states the consequence in a single sentence: 'It was therefore impossible for the RCMP to provide statistics about UAP reports.' The RCMP nonetheless told the OCSA it saw potential value in a dedicated office to which UAP reports could be referred.

Civil aviation is barely better. Transport Canada maintains the Civil Aviation Daily Occurrence Reporting System, into which NAV CANADA feeds roughly eighty percent of the content, and UAP sightings land in a category labelled 'Weather Balloon, Meteor, Rocket, UFO and Intelligence Sighting.' The report cites CTVNews.ca's January 2024 review of CADORS identifying only seventeen 2023 events that could be considered UAP, about 0.08 percent of pilot-reported incidences, and states the consequence directly: 'They are so rare in CADORS that Transport Canada is not incentivized to dedicate time and effort to explaining them. In fact, when such incidents do not raise serious safety concerns, Canadian authorities do not investigate further.' The RCAF 'does not typically investigate sightings of unexplained phenomena outside the context of investigating potential threats or distress.' The Coast Guard has a procedure, Vital Intelligence Sightings handled as MERINT reports, and used it twice between 2010 and 2022.

The report is also candid about why the scientific community stays away. It cites a survey of 1,460 tenured and tenure-track faculty at 144 research-intensive U.S. universities in which 53 percent believed UAP-related research would jeopardize their tenure or promotion, while only 7 percent held a negative opinion of such research. That gap is the mechanics of stigma quantified, and it is the same mechanism ODNI described in 2021.

Into the gap stepped civilians. Chris Rutkowski, co-founder of Ufology Research, began investigating in 1975 and has published the annual Canadian UFO Survey since 1989. From 2000 he began receiving reports directly from federal agencies including DND and Transport Canada. By 2020, the report records, 'the direct submission of UFO reports from federal departments decreased significantly,' and Ufology Research now relies primarily on public sources and access-to-information requests. A federal-to-civilian data channel that operated for twenty years quietly closed at the exact moment the topic reopened in Washington.

The fourteen recommendations are structured to rebuild the capacity Canada dismantled. Identify a federal lead, one that is 'a trusted and recognized scientific organization' with public communication capacity and an established international network: 'For example, the Canadian Space Agency could be considered for such a role.' Establish a dedicated service that collects testimonies, investigates cases and posts analyses publicly. Have Transport Canada encourage pilots, cabin crews and air traffic controllers to report without fear of stigmatization. Support public dialogue, mandate intra-governmental collaboration by internal directive, improve media relations, convene an expert panel on countering misinformation, facilitate open data, conduct periodic surveys, and support citizen science. And, internationally, 'establish partnerships with international entities dedicated to UAPs, such as AARO and NASA (U.S.A.), GEIPAN (France), and SEFAA (Chile).'

That last recommendation is where the board should slow down. The report holds up AARO, established in 2022, as a structured, transparent model, alongside NASA's September 2023 study, France's GEIPAN inside CNES since 1977, and Chile's SEFAA. Canada is being advised to plug into the American architecture at the moment that architecture is under sustained challenge from congressional witnesses who characterize AARO as a barrier rather than a bridge. If Canada builds a UAP office whose primary international relationship is with AARO, then whatever AARO does not share, Canada will not have, and Canadian access-to-information law will not reach it. During the project the OCSA received about 250 inquiries from Canadians, including requests for help interpreting photos and videos, despite the website stating it offered no such service. That is an unanswered demand signal no Canadian institution is positioned to meet.

The report states that the RCMP 'does not have a formal policy for the collection or dissemination of UAP reports,' that 'there is no classification system specific to UAPs,' that such reports are typically categorized as non-offence incidents under 'Aeronautics Act - Other Activities,' and that consequently 'It was therefore impossible for the RCMP to provide statistics about UAP reports.'

The report states that the RCMP acknowledged during consultations the growing public interest in UAPs and 'the potential value of a dedicated office responsible for providing factual information and serving as a centralized body to which UAP reports could be referred,' so the RCMP could remain focused on criminal investigations and threats to public safety.

The report states that the Royal Canadian Air Force 'does not typically investigate sightings of unexplained phenomena outside the context of investigating potential threats or distress.'

The report states that the Canadian Coast Guard handles unidentified waterborne objects under 'Vital Intelligence Sightings' procedures as MERINT reports transmitted to the nearest Canadian or U.S. coast guard station, and that from 2010 to 2022 only two MERINT reports were filed, both to the CCG's Western region.

In 1950 the Department of Transport granted engineer Wilbert Smith permission to research whether some UFOs could use the power of the Earth's magnetic field as a source of propulsion, a project called Project Magnet, which Smith expanded to include investigating the validity of UFO observations and which the Department of Transport terminated in 1954.

In 1952 the Defence Research Board established Project Second Storey, a committee chaired by NRC astronomer Dr. Peter Millman with members from Canadian military intelligence and other agencies; it held six meetings from 1952 to 1954, concluded that 'UFOs neither posed a security threat, nor were of scientific interest,' and recommended ending all investigations by the Canadian military.

In 1967 responsibility for UFO reports transferred to the National Research Council, including declassification of Project Second Storey and Project Magnet; the NRC stopped collecting UFO reports in 1995 and all related material was transferred to Library and Archives Canada, where the collection is estimated at 15,000 pages, of which some 9,500 have been digitized.

The NRC has processed about 40 UAP-related inquiries over the last decade, referring them to other government departments such as Transport Canada and Library and Archives Canada, as well as to local astronomy clubs.

Recommendation 1 states that a federal lead should be identified, that it should be 'a trusted and recognized scientific organization' with public communication capacity and an established international scientific network, and that 'For example, the Canadian Space Agency could be considered for such a role'; Recommendation 13 states that the lead organization 'should establish partnerships with international entities dedicated to UAPs, such as AARO and NASA (U.S.A.), GEIPAN (France), and SEFAA (Chile).'

The report records that independent researcher Chris Rutkowski of Ufology Research began receiving UFO reports directly from federal agencies such as DND and Transport Canada starting in 2000, but that 'by 2020, the direct submission of UFO reports from federal departments decreased significantly,' leaving Ufology Research reliant primarily on publicly available sources and formal access to information requests.

The report cites a survey of 1,460 tenured and tenure-track faculty members at 144 research-intensive universities in the United States in which 53 percent believed UAP-related research would jeopardize their tenure or promotion, even though only 7 percent had a negative opinion of this type of research.
